title: Marathon Myths We Believed for Way Too Long | The Long Run Club #203
creator: The Long Run Club
description:
Kat and Ollie go through the marathon training advice they followed for years and now think is wrong: carb loading, the 10% rule, never walking, and more.

Okay, myth number one, and this is a big one, carb loading means eating a giant bowl of pasta the night before.
Guilty, I did that for my first three marathons.
Everybody did, there were literally pasta parties at the expo.
And the problem is, one big dinner doesn't really top up your glycogen, it mostly just makes you feel heavy at the start line.
It's more like two or three days of shifting your plates toward carbs, right?
Right, two or three days, and spread out, and honestly a lot of it can be really boring food like rice and bagels.
Bagels are not boring, Kat.
Bagels are a little boring.
Myth number two, the ten percent rule.
Oh, I have feelings about this one.
So the idea is you never increase your weekly mileage by more than ten percent, and it's repeated everywhere.
And it's not terrible, it's just not based on very much.
When I was coming back from my stress fracture, ten percent was way too fast in some weeks and way too slow in others.
What actually helped was having a down week every third or fourth week, where I just cut back hard.
Yeah, the down weeks are the bit people skip, because it feels like losing fitness.
It feels terrible, you feel lazy, but it's when you actually absorb the training.
And I think the other problem with the ten percent rule is it only counts miles.
Right, it doesn't care if those miles are easy or if they're all intervals.
Ten extra easy miles and ten extra miles of hill repeats are completely different weeks.
Completely different, one of them is a nice jog and the other one is how I ended up in a boot.
So what would you tell someone building up for their first marathon?
Honestly, keep most of your running really easy, like conversation pace, and add the hard stuff slowly, one session at a time.
And listen to the small aches, because the small ache in week six is the big injury in week nine.
That should be on a t-shirt.
We should make that a t-shirt, I'm writing it down.

Okay, myth three, real runners never walk.
Here we go.
So I used to think walking in a marathon was basically failing.
Same, I'd rather have crawled than walked.
And then I paced a friend who did a run-walk method, four minutes running, one minute walking, the whole way.
And she finished faster than her previous time, right?
Eleven minutes faster, and she looked fresh at mile twenty-four while everyone around us was falling apart.
That's the thing, the walking breaks aren't really about resting, they're about not blowing up late.
And for a lot of first-timers that's the whole race, not blowing up late.
I'm not saying everybody should walk, but if you're judging people at aid stations, stop.
